about: Building materials (roadmap BT3a): Glass, Iron and steel, Concrete, and the cements (Roman and Portland, group Mortar and render). Fields as bidb/building_materials.py.

materials.name: Window glass

period.text: AD 43, the Roman conquest: Roman villas in Britain had glazed windows (window glass found at Carsington); after the Romans left it is found again from the late 7th century, with the first churches and monasteries; still in use

materials.technology: Glass was taxed as a luxury: the window tax (England and Wales 1696, Scotland 1748, Ireland 1799; all repealed in 1851) and the glass excise (Great Britain 1746, on finished glass including windows from 1811, abolished in 1845; Ireland 1825-1845).

examples.name: Carsington Roman Villa
examples.note: Small glazed windows with shutters; window glass found in the excavations

materials.note: The individual ways of making window glass follow as their own entries (broad sheet, crown, sheet, plate and float glass).

materials.name: Stained glass

period.text: 675, the earliest known reference: Benedict Biscop's glaziers from France at Monkwearmouth (coloured glass of the late 7th century found there and at Jarrow); most medieval windows were smashed at the Reformation and the craft died out in England until the Gothic Revival of the early 19th century; still made

materials.technology: Brought in: Benedict Biscop fetched glassmakers from Francia, who worked at Monkwearmouth. The Reformation's destruction ended the craft in England; the Catholic and Gothic revival and the church building of the 19th century revived it.

examples.name: St Paul's Church, Jarrow
examples.note: Anglo-Saxon chancel window made up from excavated fragments, called the oldest stained glass window in the world

materials.note: The Monkwearmouth-Jarrow article dates the Jarrow fragments to 'about AD 600', which is before the monastery was founded (674/682); the stained glass article dates the finds to the late 7th century.

materials.name: Broad sheet (cylinder) glass

period.text: 1226, when broad sheet glass was first made in the isles, at Chiddingfold in the Weald; making it there slowly declined and ceased by the early 16th century (about 1525)

regions.text: The Weald: Chiddingfold, Surrey, on the border with Sussex

materials.technology: A blown cylinder cut open and flattened on an iron plate; small, imperfect, mostly translucent pieces set in lead. The Weald had suitable sand, bracken ash for the alkali and beech charcoal for the kiln.

examples.name: Westminster Abbey
examples.note: An order was placed for Wealden broad glass

materials.note: Romans made window glass by the same muff (cylinder) process from the late 3rd century. Leadlight says domestic windows were of broad or cylinder glass until crown glass was first made in England in 1678, so broad glass was still glazed after Wealden making ended (imported glass: cylinder glass came from France and Germany in the 18th century). The 19th-century cylinder blown sheet is 'Sheet glass'.

materials.name: Crown glass

period.text: 1678, when crown glass was first made in London (the technique came from Normandy in the 17th century); it dominated window glass until the 19th century, and the hand-blown methods lasted at least until the end of the 19th century (about 1900)

regions.text: London from 1678; later St Helens (St Helens Crown Glass Company, 1826) and Smethwick (Chance's Spon Lane works, a crown glass works bought in 1822)

materials.technology: A blown globe spun flat into a disc up to 5-6 feet across, cut into small panes (the thick centre, the bullseye, for cheap windows); the method was kept a trade secret by Venice and Normandy. Taxed by the glass excise (1746-1845) and, through the windows it filled, the window tax (1696-1851).

materials.name: Sheet glass (cylinder blown sheet)

period.text: 1832, when Chance Brothers made the first British cylinder blown sheet glass; machine-drawn cylinder sheet was made under licence by Pilkington from 1910; float glass replaced the older methods once it sold at full scale from 1960

materials.technology: French and Belgian glassblowers brought the cylinder process; Paxton's order for a large greenhouse at Chatsworth led Chance to make very long panes (about 1848), and so to the Crystal Palace, whose plan was set by the size of the pane.

examples.name: The Crystal Palace
examples.note: 293,000 panes by Chance Brothers, the largest then available (10 by 49 inches); destroyed 1936

materials.name: Polished plate glass

period.text: 1773, when the British Cast Plate Glass Company was authorised at Ravenhead, St Helens (blown plate had been made in London since the 1620s, for mirrors and coach plates); rolled plate followed in 1847; replaced by float glass once it sold at full scale from 1960

materials.technology: Cast on an iron table, then ground flat and polished, an expensive process; a casting hall built by French technicians from St Gobain. James Hartley's rolled plate (1847) roofed railway stations.
materials.note: The History of St Helens gives 1773 for the company's authorisation and its casting hall, the St Helens article 1786 for its operations there. Hartley's rolled plate patent is dated 1838 by the Architectural glass article, 1847 by History of glass.

materials.name: Float glass

period.text: 1959, when float glass was launched in the UK (developed 1953-1957 at Pilkington's Cowley Hill Works, St Helens; full-scale profitable sales from 1960); now most of the world's flat glass

regions.text: Invented at St Helens, Lancashire; licensed worldwide in the 1960s

materials.technology: Molten glass poured onto a bath of molten tin flows flat under its own weight, giving a smooth face on both sides without grinding or polishing.

materials.name: Sash window

period.text: The 1670s, the oldest surviving examples (Palace House, Newmarket, and Ham House); common in Georgian and Victorian houses, and still made

materials.technology: Sliding sashes balanced by hidden weights on cords over pulleys; late Victorian and Edwardian suburban houses used standard units about 4 feet wide.

materials.name: Wrought iron

period.text: About 800 BC, the start of the British Iron Age (the bloomery made wrought iron directly from ore); a structural material from the puddling process of 1784 until the 1880s; the last puddling works, Atlas Forge in Bolton, closed in 1973 (some is still recycled from scrap for restoration)

materials.technology: Bloomery, then finery forge; Henry Cort's puddling furnace (1784) made it with coal instead of charcoal and cheap enough for beams, bridges and rails; cheap Bessemer and open-hearth steel replaced it.

examples.name: Palm House, Kew Gardens

materials.name: Cast iron

period.text: About 1500: FISH dates cast iron from the 15th century, and in England it was first cast for cannon and shot in the Reformation (Wealden blast furnaces); a structural material from the Iron Bridge (1779) until it was replaced by steel in about 1900

regions.text: The Weald (until the 1760s), then Shropshire (Coalbrookdale) and the coalfields

materials.technology: Abraham Darby's coke smelting at Coalbrookdale (1709) and steam-pumped blast from 1743 made it cheap; strong in compression but brittle in tension, so columns and arches. Bridge failures (Dee 1847, Tay 1879, Norwood Junction 1891) ended its use under railways.

materials.name: Iron frame (fireproof construction)

period.text: 1797, Ditherington Flax Mill, Shrewsbury (built 1796-1797), the first iron-framed building; cast-iron columns became usual in mills, warehouses and commercial buildings until steel replaced them in about 1900

materials.name: Steel

period.text: 1856, Bessemer's patent, which first made steel cheap enough to build with (steel had been made in small amounts since the Iron Age, at Broxmouth 490-375 BC, and by cementation in England from about 1614); the Forth Bridge (1882-1890) was the first major structure in Britain built of it; still the main structural metal

materials.technology: The Bessemer converter cut the price from £40 to £6-7 a ton; brittle Bessemer steel gave way to Siemens-Martin open-hearth steel for structures, and open hearth had superseded Bessemer in the UK by 1900. Basic oxygen steelmaking replaced both from the 1950s.

materials.name: Steel frame

period.text: 1896, when the Royal Insurance Building in Liverpool (erected 1896-1903), the first to use a steel frame in the United Kingdom, was begun; in London the Savoy Hotel extension (1903-1904) came first; still the usual frame of large buildings

materials.technology: Cheap structural steel; the frame carries the floors and walls so that masonry is only a facing, and rooms can be free of columns. The early London frames used American materials and engineers such as Sven Bylander.

materials.name: Portland cement

period.text: 1824, Joseph Aspdin's patent of 21 October 1824 (the name is in a directory of 1823); modern Portland cement came from William Aspdin's work of the 1840s and Isaac Charles Johnson's; now the usual cement of mortar and concrete

regions.text: Leeds and Wakefield (Aspdin, 1825); the Thames: Rotherhithe (William Aspdin, 1843) and Swanscombe (Johnson); later Gateshead

materials.technology: Grew out of Smeaton's hydraulic-lime experiments (1756) and the natural cements; limestone and clay burnt to clinker at a higher heat. The 1859 London sewer specification set its standard, and the rotary kiln (Ransome, 1885) made it stronger and more uniform.
materials.note: Who invented 'true' Portland cement is disputed: Joseph Aspdin's 1824 cement was 'nothing like modern Portland cement'; his son William is regarded as the inventor of modern Portland cement; Isaac Charles Johnson claimed to be, and is 'generally recognised as such'.

materials.name: Mass concrete

period.text: In Britain the name for early unreinforced concrete cast in situ, used mainly between 1850 and 1900 (the years a source gives); Glenfinnan Viaduct, built 1897-1901, is of it

materials.technology: Concrete poured into shuttering, strong in compression but weak in tension: walls, and works that need weight, such as dams, reservoirs, retaining walls and harbours; arches carried the loads.

sources.title: Mass concrete
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Historically, in Britain, mass concrete designated early concrete with no reinforcement cast in situ using shuttering. It was used mainly between 1850 and 1900 on a variety of buildings, mainly as a walling material or where mass was required for gravity such as in dams, reservoirs, retaining walls and maritime structures.
